(B) **my big fatggreek wedding** - Just removes a space and duplicates a letter, not humorous

(C) **my big fat greek weeding** - Changes "wedding" to "weeding" - this is a clever pun/homophone joke! The word sounds similar but has a completely different meaning (removing weeds vs. a marriage ceremony)

(D) **my big fat greek wedading** - Just a garbled misspelling, not humorous

The answer is **(C)** because substituting "weeding" for "wedding" creates a humorous play on words. The two words are homophones/near-homophones, so it's a clever pun that evokes the absurd image of a Greek "weeding" instead of a wedding.
